implementation_notes: C has neither a deadline nor a cancellation type in its standard library, so the pattern is hand-wired: take one absolute deadline as a struct timespec from clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) at ingress, thread it through the per-request context every call receives, and derive a relative timeout for each blocking wait - poll(2)/epoll_wait take milliseconds, so compute remaining and pass it instead of -1 (infinite). CLOCK_MONOTONIC is never affected by discontinuous wall-clock jumps, which is exactly what budget arithmetic needs. For cancellation, prefer an explicit done flag or an eventfd checked between stages over pthread_cancel, whose asynchronous cancellation is only safe in code that was written for it.
idiom_name: absolute CLOCK_MONOTONIC deadline + remaining-time timeouts for poll/ppoll
pitfalls: Using CLOCK_REALTIME for the deadline: an NTP step or manual clock change makes remaining time jump or go negative - use CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
ppoll(2) takes a relative struct timespec while pselect(2) takes an absolute one; mixing the idioms produces waits that ignore the deadline or fire immediately.
pthread_cancel is asynchronous and can fire inside a critical section or while a mutex is held; propagate an explicit check (or eventfd) unless all code is cancellation-safe.
The deadline value must be immutable per request; a struct shared across threads that is written by one of them races - compute remaining locally in each thread instead.
'No deadline' must not be encoded as 0: poll(0) returns immediately. Represent it explicitly (negative/infinite) or the hop silently drops the budget.
